This is India.
A land of snow-capped mountains and burning deserts, of mighty rivers and endless coastlines.
Home to more than a billion people, hundreds of languages, and one of the oldest civilisations on Earth.
Here, empires rose and fell. Great kings built magnificent cities and fought legendary wars.
Religions were born here. Ideas sailed across oceans. And traders, travellers and invaders all left their mark.
It is a story that stretches back hundreds of thousands of years.

And in this series, we will tell it from the very beginning. From the Stone Age, to the Indus cities, the Mauryas and the Guptas, the Cholas, the Sultans and the Mughals, all the way to the British Raj and Independence.
Over more than one hundred episodes. In order. One chapter at a time.
Welcome to India: The Full Story.
No newspapers. No cameras. No written history books.
So how do we know what happened in India thousands of years ago?
The answer is simple. We become detectives. And the past has left us clues everywhere.
Historians divide these clues into two big groups. Archaeological sources, the things people left behind. And literary sources, the words they wrote down.
Let's begin with the oldest clues of all.
In the hills of Madhya Pradesh lie the rock shelters of Bhimbetka.
Painted on their walls are hunters, dancers and animals. Some of these paintings are more than ten thousand years old.
They show us how India's earliest people lived, long before anyone could write.
Next, come the ruined cities.
In 1921, archaeologists digging at Harappa uncovered the remains of a vast and ancient city.
A year later came Mohenjo-daro, with its brick houses, covered drains, and the famous Great Bath.
These cities are more than four and a half thousand years old.
Thousands of small stone seals were found here too, carved with animals and a mysterious script.
That script has never been deciphered. It remains one of history's great unsolved puzzles.
Then there are inscriptions: words carved into stone and metal.
Emperor Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks and pillars across his vast empire.
But for centuries, no one could read them.
Then in 1837, a British scholar named James Prinsep cracked the ancient Brahmi script, and Ashoka's voice was heard again.
The lion capital from his pillar at Sarnath is today the national emblem of India.
Coins are another treasure.
India's earliest coins were small pieces of silver, stamped with symbols. We call them punch-marked coins.
Coins tell us who ruled, what they believed, and how far their trade reached.

Across South India, hoards of Roman gold and silver coins have been found. And at the port of Arikamedu, near Puducherry, Roman pottery proves that India traded with Rome about two thousand years ago.
Now, the second group of clues: literary sources.
The oldest is the Rigveda, a collection of hymns composed more than three thousand years ago.
Buddhist texts like the Jataka tales, and Jain texts, describe the kingdoms and daily life of their times.
Some books are not religious at all. Kautilya's Arthashastra is a guide to running a kingdom.
And in the far south, the Sangam poems of Tamil Nadu sing of kings, trade and love.
Finally, there are the tales of foreign travellers.
Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador, described the court of Chandragupta Maurya in his book, Indica.
The Chinese pilgrims Fa-Hien and Xuanzang walked thousands of kilometres to visit India's Buddhist sites.
And the scholar Al-Biruni wrote a detailed account of India in the eleventh century.
No single clue tells the whole story.
But put them together, like the pieces of a puzzle, and the past begins to speak.
